Your deposit is held at **Truist Bank in Gainesville**, in a separate account, and it does **not** earn interest. The lease says so directly: "The Landlord keeps the deposit in a separate account at Truist Bank in Gainesville that does not earn interest" (Room Rental Agreement, Security Deposit section).

That setup is lawful. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(1)(a), a landlord may hold a deposit in a separate non-interest-bearing account at a Florida financial institution, as long as the money is not commingled with the landlord's own funds or used by the landlord before it is due. Interest is required only if the landlord chooses a different option: an interest-bearing account under § 83.49(1)(b), or a surety bond under § 83.49(1)(c). Because the landlord chose the non-interest-bearing account, you are not owed interest on this deposit.

Two things are not settled by the lease:

- **Bank address.** Section 83.49(2)(b) requires the written notice to state the "name and address" of the depository. The lease gives the bank's name and city but no street address. If the lease counts as that notice, the city-level description may be enough. If the address requirement is not met, the statute does not say the deposit is forfeited. It does say that a failure to give this notice is "not a defense to the payment of rent when due" (§ 83.49(2)). Whether a missing address matters in any other way is not something I can settle from the statute alone.
- **Florida location.** Section 83.49(1)(a) requires a Florida financial institution. The lease says "Gainesville," which suggests a Florida branch, but you can check the bank's branch locator to confirm.

The answer to the interest question would change only if the landlord gave you a separate written notice that the deposit was in an interest-bearing account. Nothing in the lease suggests that.

Yes, you can tell your landlord, and the lease tells you how. For an emergency such as "no air conditioning in summer," the Repairs section (p. 2) says to **call** Patricia Nguyen at (352) 555-0198 and not just text. Call first, then send a text or email afterward so you have a written record. The Notices section (p. 2) allows day-to-day messages by text or email. Note what you said on the call, the date, and the time.

The lease says the landlord "will try to fix ordinary problems within a week." That is the landlord's stated goal, not a legal deadline, so a missed week does not by itself give you rights.

**Where the law comes in**

- Under Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a), the landlord must comply with applicable building, housing, and health codes. I can't confirm from the statute text whether a local code requires working air conditioning in Gainesville. If it does, the landlord's duty under this subsection is stronger. If it doesn't, the duty may not reach an AC failure at all. This point is unsettled and needs a check of the local code.
- If the problem is treated as a material failure to maintain, § 83.56(1) lets you terminate, but only after you deliver a written notice that names the problem and states your intent to terminate, and the landlord has 7 days to fix it. If the unit is untenantable and you move out, you owe no rent for that period (§ 83.56(1)(a)). If you stay, the rent is reduced in proportion to the lost rental value (§ 83.56(1)(b)).
- Be careful with rent. Under § 83.56(5)(a), if you pay rent knowing about the problem, you may give up your right to terminate or sue over that problem, though not over a later or continuing one. If you want to keep those rights, put your complaint in writing before the next rent is due.

- If a local code requires AC, your position is stronger under § 83.51(1)(a).

**Generally no.** Your landlord may enter your room only in limited situations, and in most of them must give you notice first.

**The rule.** Part II of chapter 83 covers your room. It is a part of a structure rented as a home or sleeping place, and the educational-services exclusion in § 83.42(1) is for residency incidental to educational services, which doesn't describe a private room rental like yours. Under § 83.53(2), a landlord may enter for repairs only on "reasonable notice," which means at least 24 hours before the entry, and only between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

**Your lease is stricter, and that controls.** The "Landlord's Entry" section says the landlord "will enter the Tenant's room only for repairs or inspections, after giving at least 24 hours' notice by text, between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., unless there is an emergency." The lease allows a narrower window than the statute, so the 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. window applies to you. The lease also says day-to-day messages may be sent by text, so a text counts as notice.

**The exceptions.** The landlord may enter without advance notice in these cases:
- **Emergency.** Section 83.53(2)(b) allows entry in an emergency, and the lease says "unless there is an emergency." The lease gives examples: a leak, no air conditioning in summer, or a sparking outlet.
- **Protection or preservation of the premises.** Section 83.53(2) allows entry "at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises." This is not clearly limited to emergencies. Whether a particular visit falls under it is unsettled. A reading that favors you is that it covers only urgent threats to the house. A reading that favors the landlord is that it covers any step taken to protect the property, which would allow broader entry.
- **Your consent.** Section 83.53(2)(a) allows entry with your consent. You may not unreasonably refuse consent to an inspection or repair entry under § 83.53(1).
- **Your absence.** Under § 83.53(2)(d), if you are away for half of your rental-payment period, the landlord may enter. If your rent is current and you told the landlord in advance that you would be away, the landlord may enter only with your consent or to protect the premises.

**Limits on the landlord even when entry is allowed.** Under § 83.53(3), the landlord "shall not abuse the right of access nor use it to harass the tenant." The lease's shared-area rule ("at any time") does not extend to your room.

**How this changes the answer.** If the landlord gave you a text at least 24 hours ahead, came in between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., and it was for a repair or inspection, the entry was likely allowed. If there was no advance text and no emergency, the entry likely broke both the lease and § 83.53(2).

**Question:** Did Ms. Nguyen text you at least 24 hours before she came into your room, and about what time did she come in?

Management generally must give you **at least 24 hours' notice** before entering your apartment. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.53(2), that notice is "reasonable notice" for repairs, and entry for repairs must happen between **7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.** Your lease says the same thing in Section 14.2: at least 24 hours' notice, by email to the address on your resident portal account or by a written notice left on the Unit's front door, and entry only between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.

Several situations change this:

- **Emergency:** No notice is required. Lease § 14.4 and Fla. Stat. § 83.53(2)(b) allow entry at any time.
- **Protection or preservation of the property:** The statute allows entry "at any time" for this purpose (§ 83.53(2)). Lease § 14.4 also allows entry without notice to protect or preserve the Community.
- **Your consent:** If you agree to a specific entry, notice terms do not apply (§ 83.53(2)(a); Lease § 14.1).
- **Your maintenance request:** Lease § 14.3 says that if you submit a maintenance request, you authorize entry for that repair "without further notice" during the 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. hours. Whether that clause can waive the 24-hour notice is unsettled. The statute does not mention waiver, and Lease § 39.1 voids any lease term that conflicts with Florida law. On one reading, your portal request is your consent and the clause is enforceable. On the other, the statute's 24-hour requirement still applies, so the clause is void to that extent.
- **Absence:** If you are away for one-half of a rent period, the landlord may enter (§ 83.53(2)(d); Lease § 14.4). If your rent is current and you told the landlord about the absence, the landlord may enter only with your consent or to protect the property (§ 83.53(2)).
- **Inspections:** Lease § 14.5 allows one inspection per semester and one before move-out. The statute's notice rules still apply, and the lease requires a written note left in the Unit after each entry.

Also, § 83.53(3) bars the landlord from abusing its access rights or using them to harass you.

**Short answer: the lease does not clearly prohibit a space heater, so you probably can use an electric one, but the lease's fire rules leave some room for the landlord to object.**

The lease never mentions space heaters. The closest rule is Addendum A, Section A-5.1, which bans "[c]andles, incense, oil lamps, and other open flames" in the Unit. Whether an electric heater counts as an "open flame" is unsettled:

- **Reading that allows it:** An electric heater has no flame, so it is not an "open flame" under A-5.1. Nothing else in the lease bars it.
- **Reading that restricts it:** The landlord could argue that a heater is a fire hazard of the kind A-5.1 and the fire-safety rules were meant to cover. Under this reading, the landlord could treat it as a policy violation. The lease does not list a charge for that, so any remedy would be under Section 19.1 (Community Policies) or 26.2 (other defaults, with written notice under Section 83.56(2)).

Whatever the answer on the flame question, these rules apply:

- **Damage:** You must pay for damage you or your guests cause, other than normal wear and tear (Sections 13.5 and 22.1).

- **Fire equipment:** Tampering with fire equipment carries a $250 charge plus repair cost (Addendum A, Section A-5.3; Addendum N).

If the heater burns fuel, such as kerosene, propane, or any heater with a real flame, A-5.1 very likely applies and you should not use it.

If you are using the heater because the bedroom does not heat properly, that is a separate issue. Repairs to the heating system are the landlord's duty under Section 13.4 and Florida Statute 83.51, and you must report the problem through the portal (Section 13.1).

**No. The lease does not allow you to sublease your room for the summer.** Section 23.1 says: "You may not sublet your Bedroom or any part of the Unit, whether for the summer or any other period, and you may not let anyone else live in your Bedroom in exchange for payment. Any sublease is void and is a default under this Lease." Addendum H-1 repeats that subletting is not allowed. Because the lease names summer subleases specifically, I don't see a reading under which one is permitted.

I could not find a subletting rule in the Part II sections I searched. Florida's general subletting rule is not in the part of Chapter 83 I can access, so I can't check it. That doesn't change the answer, because Section 39.1 makes the lease govern unless it conflicts with Florida law, and I found no Florida law in my sources that overrides Section 23.1. The lease clause is the controlling rule here.

The consequences are serious. A sublease would be void, and it would be a default under Section 23.1. Under Section 26.2, the landlord could then give you written notice under Section 83.56(2). Section 26.3 also says the landlord may recover rent and other amounts that Florida law allows.

Your lease does give you one route to leave your room before the End Date. Under Section 23.2 and Addendum H, you can arrange a lease transfer to a replacement resident:

- **Approval:** The replacement must apply, meet the current rental standards, and be approved by Manager (H-2.2). The landlord does not promise to find one (H-2.1).
- **Replacement's lease:** The replacement signs a new lease for the rest of the term at the current installment amount and pays the security deposit, administrative fee, and amenity fee then in effect (H-2.3).
- **Fee:** You pay a $300.00 transfer fee, or $450.00 if the landlord found the replacement from its transfer list (H-2.4).
- **Your account:** All amounts you owe through the transfer date must be paid first (H-2.5).
- **Your release:** You are released from future rent only on the date the replacement's lease begins and after you return all keys and access cards. Until then you remain responsible for all rent (H-3).

A transfer of this kind would not be a sublease, but you would stay liable until the replacement's lease starts. Whether a transfer works for a summer depends on the dates. Your lease runs from August 15, 2026 to July 31, 2027 (Section 3.1).

**Call the after-hours maintenance line at (352) 555-0177.** Paragraph 10 of your lease says that for "a repair that cannot wait, such as a water leak, a sewer backup, or a loss of air conditioning," you should call that number. The statute also requires a landlord of a duplex to keep the plumbing in reasonable working condition and the structure in good repair (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(b)). Your lease does not change that for a duplex, since ¶9 is the landlord's obligation and nothing in the lease shifts it to you.

Lease ¶9 has a similar exception for damage caused by the tenant, and ¶11 makes you responsible for changing the AC filter every month. If the filter was the cause, the landlord could argue the repair is yours. If the cause is an equipment failure, the repair is the landlord's.

Two cautions from the lease:
- Do not hire your own repair person and bill the landlord unless the landlord approves in writing (Lease ¶10).
- Keep a record of when you called, whom you spoke with, and what they said. Lease ¶20 requires written notices to the landlord to go by hand delivery or certified mail to the listed address, so a phone call may not count as formal written notice. Send a written follow-up to that address if the repair is delayed.

Paragraph 5 states that the landlord "will hold the deposit in a separate interest-bearing account at Merchants and Southern Bank, Gainesville, Florida, and Tenant will receive interest at the rate required by Florida law." Under Fla. Stat. § 83.49(1)(b), a landlord who uses an interest-bearing account must pay the tenant either at least 75 percent of the account's annualized average interest rate or 5 percent per year simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord makes that election, so I can't tell you the amount until we know the bank's rate and which option the landlord picked.

- **Payment timing.** Under § 83.49(9), interest must be paid to you directly, or credited against the current month's rent, at least once a year.

**The statute.** Fla. Stat. § 83.53(2) says "reasonable notice" for repair entry "is notice given at least 24 hours prior to the entry," and that repair entry must fall between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Under § 83.47(1)(a), a lease provision that purports to waive or preclude the rights in this part is void to the extent of that conflict. So for a repair, the 12-hour term does not bind you, and the landlord must give 24 hours.

The 24-hour figure in § 83.53(2) is written only for repairs. The statute does not give a fixed notice period for inspections or showings. So:
- Reading one: the lease's 12 hours is an agreed term that governs these entries, and you can rely on it.
- Reading two: the landlord must still give "reasonable notice," and 12 hours may or may not meet that standard depending on the circumstances. A court would decide.

**Yes, you can end the lease early, but the cost depends on an open legal question.**

**What the lease says.** Paragraph 18 lets a tenant end the lease early by giving the landlord at least 60 days' written notice and paying a $2,200.00 early termination fee (two months' rent) by the day the tenant moves out. If both steps are done, the tenant owes no rent for any period after moving out and returning the keys. If either step is missed, the tenant "remains liable for rent through the end of the term, less any rent Landlord receives from a new tenant" (Lease ¶18). Notice must be in writing and delivered by hand to the landlord's office or sent by certified mail to Hawthorne Rentals, Inc., 1702 NW 13th Street, Suite 4, Gainesville, FL 32609, or to P.O. Box 14077, Gainesville, FL 32604 (Lease ¶20). Both tenants signed and are each responsible for the whole rent and every promise in the lease (Lease p. 1).

**The open question: is the $2,200 fee enforceable?** Florida law allows a landlord to charge an early termination fee of no more than two months' rent, with no more than 60 days' notice, only if the tenant "indicated acceptance" by signing a separate addendum with a checkbox provision (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). The lease you have contains no such addendum. The lease has no checkbox for early termination, and the initials lines on every page are blank. Paragraph 23 says the lease is the entire agreement.

- **Reading A (fee not enforceable):** Because no separate signed addendum exists, the landlord cannot use the fee under § 83.595(4). The landlord would be limited to the other remedies in § 83.595. Those are holding you liable for rent as it comes due (§ 83.595(3)), or retaking the unit and reletting it for your account, with a duty to relet in good faith and credit the new rent against what you owe (§ 83.595(2)). Under this reading, your cost is rent until the unit is re-rented or the lease ends, not a flat $2,200.
- **Reading B (fee enforceable as a contract term):** Paragraph 18 is a written agreement, and § 83.595 says what the landlord "may" do but does not clearly void a fee agreed to in the lease. The landlord could argue the $2,200 is owed if you follow ¶18 exactly. Under this reading, following ¶18 costs $2,200 plus rent through your move-out date.

I can't tell you which reading a court would adopt, so the answer is unsettled. Under either reading, following ¶18 exactly (60 days' written notice delivered per ¶20, and the $2,200 paid by move-out) is the path that gives the landlord the least basis to claim more. Whether the fee is owed in practice depends on whether the landlord will accept it, so you may want to ask the landlord in writing whether they will apply ¶18 as written.

**No, not under this lease.** The lease gives you no early termination fee option. In section 16, the early termination box is unchecked, and the lease states: "[X] This lease does not include an early termination option. If Tenant moves out early, Tenant is responsible for rent as Florida law provides."

Florida law allows an early termination fee only if the tenant agreed to it in a separate signed addendum. Under Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4), the landlord may charge an early termination fee only if the landlord and tenant indicated acceptance "at the time the rental agreement was made," and the tenant accepted it "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement." Your lease has no such addendum, and the fee box in section 16 is blank and unchecked. So the fee route is not available on the lease as written.

If you move out early, the landlord's remedies come from § 83.595, which applies when a tenant abandons the unit or surrenders possession. The landlord may choose one of these:
- **Terminate and retake the unit** (§ 83.595(1)). This ends your further liability for rent.
- **Relet the unit for your account** (§ 83.595(2)). You owe the difference between the lease rent and what the landlord recovers from re-renting. The landlord must make a good-faith effort to relet, and rent received is credited against what you owe.
- **Stand by and hold you liable for rent as it comes due** (§ 83.595(3)). You owe rent as it falls due through the lease term.

Under § 83.595(a), the landlord can also recover rent accrued through the end of the month in which it retakes possession, plus damage charges.

Section 15 is a separate matter. It requires 30 days' written notice before the lease ends and sets $975 as liquidated damages if you move out on the end date without that notice. That clause concerns moving out at the end of the term, not ending the lease early.

**Open question:** If you signed a separate addendum about early termination or liquidated damages, the answer could change. Such an addendum could make a specific fee enforceable, subject to the statute's limit of two months' rent. The lease you gave me has no such addendum, so I have assumed none exists.
